# R5 — Great High Priest 4:14–5:10; Regression 5:11–6:3; Warning 6:4–8; Assurance 6:9–12; Abraham Oath 6:13–20

**Range read in full:** source lines 2384–2735 (slice `R5_highpriest_4_14-6_20_2384-2735.txt`)  
**Source:** Gareth Lee Cockerill, *The Epistle to the Hebrews* (NICNT, 2012)  
**Evidence class default:** Cockerill (commentator) on Hebrews; translation of Hebrews in Cockerill’s running text is his own.  
**Coverage note:** Body exposition of II.A–B read sequentially. Footnote apparatus appears largely stripped in the cache slice; no explicit labels “Wesleyan,” “Arminian,” or “Reformed” appear in the body text of this range. Cockerill’s constructive reading of 6:4–8 (genuine conversion + real irreversible apostasy + same-land-can-produce-thorns) is extracted fully and is the functional opposite of common “never-truly-saved” / purely-hypothetical-warning construals he rules out by argument.

**Suggested page targets:** `hebrews`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`, `hebrews-warning-passages`, `priesthood-of-christ`, `abraham`, `melchizedek`, `atonement`

## Claims

### C1 — Macro-section: High Priest as resource and urgency for perseverance (4:14–10:18)
**Locus:** 2386  
**Quote:** "Thus in Heb 4:14-10:18 the pastor describes the Son as the all-sufficient High Priest and the fully adequate resource for perseverance in faithful obedience."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) After the wilderness unfaithful and the accountability word of 4:12–13, 4:14–10:18 presents the Son’s high priesthood as both fulfillment of prior revelation and God’s provision to avoid the disobedient’s fate; those who use that provision join the faithful of 10:19–12:29 toward the “Unshakable Kingdom” (12:28). Target pages: `hebrews`, `priesthood-of-christ`.

### C2 — Four-part / two-pair structure of 4:14–10:18
**Locus:** 2388–2390  
**Quote:** "This section is best divided into four parts - 4:14-5:10; 5:11-6:20; 7:1-28; and 8:1-10:18 - that can be grouped into two pairs."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Pair one (4:14–5:10; 5:11–6:20) reopens the divine conversation of 1:1–2:18, introduces high priesthood, and prepares embrace of the Son as High Priest; pair two (7:1–28; 8:1–10:18) expounds majesty/sufficiency by completing Father–Son conversation. Target pages: `hebrews`, `priesthood-of-christ`.

### C3 — Aaronic typology foundation; Ps 110:4 and Ps 40:6–8 itinerary
**Locus:** 2392  
**Quote:** "To this exhortation he joins a comparison/ contrast that establishes a typological relationship between Aaron's high priesthood and that of the Son of God (5:1-10). This typology is fundamental to the argument of both 7:1-28 and 8:1-10:18."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) 5:1–10’s Aaron–Christ typology undergirds 7 and 8–10; 5:11–6:20 arouses hearers before exposition of Ps 110:4 (6:20); 8:1–10:18 develops 5:1–3, 7–10 contrasts, with Ps 40:6–8 (Heb 10:5–10) as heart: Son accepts Ps 110:4 appointment by incarnate obedience, fulfilling Ps 2:7 sonship. Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `melchizedek`, `hebrews`.

### C4 — Father–Son conversation pattern: 7 // 1 and 8–10 // 2
**Locus:** 2394  
**Quote:** "In 7:1-28 the Father addresses the Son as the eternal, exalted High Priest. In 8:1-10:18 the Son answers by affirming his incarnate obedience (10:5-10) as the means by which he has accepted this Father-given vocation"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) 7:1–28 : 8:1–10:18 :: 1:1–14 : 2:5–18 — Father’s address of exalted status answered by Son’s incarnate obedience as means of exaltation/vocation. Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `hebrews`.

### C5 — 4:14–16: two “since we have… therefore let us…” arguments; Christology serves exhortation
**Locus:** 2406, 2410  
**Quote:** "With three sentences he offers the people of God two similarly structured arguments, taking the form \"Since we have .... therefore let us ...\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) First argument (v. 14) resumes hold-fast from wilderness narrative; second (vv. 15–16) points forward to high-priestly provision for access—means of holding fast. High-priestly exposition is not speculation but Christological foundation for exhortation; themes reverse in 10:19–25. Target pages: `hebrews`, `priesthood-of-christ`.

### C6 — “Great high priest” redundancy; through the heavens as continuing access
**Locus:** 2414–2416  
**Quote:** "there is redundancy in the expression \"great high priest\": one might say, \"great great priest\" or \"high high priest.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “Great” intensifies immeasurable superiority over Levitical priests; perfect participle “who has gone through the heavens” = Aaron through the veil → Christ into God’s presence, with continuing validity—access is present reality for the people. Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `hebrews`.

### C7 — Hold fast to confession: content + public profession
**Locus:** 2420  
**Quote:** "This term refers first of all to the content of our confession, the substance of \"the faith\" we profess - belief in the uniqueness and saving efficacy of Jesus Christ; and, secondly, to our public profession of that faith."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “Hold fast” = tenacious endurance in profession; high-priesthood teaching fortifies belief so hearers continue a life that professes faith in Jesus as Son and effective High Priest. Target pages: `hebrews`, `priesthood-of-christ`.

### C8 — Sympathy stronger than English “sympathize”; active assistance vs Aaronic “deal gently”
**Locus:** 2426  
**Quote:** "This is a \"sympathy\" that leads to active assistance. It finds expression and is embodied in the grace of forgiveness and victory over temptation that this High Priest ministers"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Greek sympathy-bond implies empowering help in “weaknesses” (human limitations making temptation possible); Aaronic high priest can only “deal gently” / put up with sinners because himself “subject to weakness” and sinful (5:2). Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `hebrews`.

### C9 — Tempted in every way without sin: lifelong perfect; not limited to fear of suffering
**Locus:** 2428–2432  
**Quote:** "the emphatic \"in every way, just as we are\" makes it impossible to restrict Jesus' temptation to the fear of suffering. … He experienced temptation as we do, but he did not re spond as we do - he never yielded."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Perfect “has been tempted” = lifelong endurance culminating in death, benefits still available; temptation includes sinful pleasures and fear of hardship; “without sin” is verdict on incarnate course, not mere preincarnate sinlessness—obedience perfects him as “source of eternal salvation” (5:8–10). Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `atonement`, `hebrews`.

### C10 — Bold approach to throne of grace: OT fear → Christ-authorized confidence
**Locus:** 2434–2438  
**Quote:** "God's people are urged to draw near to the true heavenly \"throne\" of God \"with confidence\" because their High Priest has made that \"throne\" a throne \"of grace,\" a true \"mercy seat,\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Under OC only high priest approached the Ark-throne yearly in fear (judgment); through Christ’s obedient sacrifice consciences are cleansed (9:14) so holy God is approachable. “Confidence” is authorization, not mere feeling. “Mercy” = forgiveness/covenant love; “grace” = redemptive power (2:9; Spirit 10:29) for overcoming temptation—timely, always available help to hold the confession. Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `atonement`, `hebrews`.

### C11 — 5:1–10 structure: OT priest (present tense) vs Christ (aorists); chiastic effectiveness/humanity/sacrifice/appointment
**Locus:** 2452–2460  
**Quote:** "While vv. 4/5-6 compare and contrast these priests with reference to their divine appointment, vv. 1-3/7-10 compare and contrast them in regard to their effectiveness (vv. 2a, 9), their humanity and its relationship to sin (vv. 2b, 8), and their sacrifices (vv. 3, 7)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) No Gentile-priesthood concern or Jerusalem-Temple corruption polemic; OT portrait shaped to prefigure Son and show old’s ineffectiveness necessitating new. Movement: every high priest → Melchizedekian High Priest; offered for himself → offered himself; beset with weakness → learned obedience; deal gently → Source of eternal salvation. Foundation for 7:1–10:18. Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `melchizedek`, `hebrews`.

### C12 — Aaronic impotence: “deal gently” only; ignorant/going astray vs those who obey
**Locus:** 2468–2472  
**Quote:** "Although Christ is able to \"sympathize\" (4:15) with and deliver his people from their sinful \"weakness,\" the Aaronic high priest can only \"deal gently\" (NIV) with the sinner. … He has no ability to deliver them from sin"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) First contrast = effectiveness: Aaron restrains anger; may be limited to sins of ignorance (cf. 9:7); “ignorant and going astray” also names people’s tendency under old ministry. Christ is “Author of eternal salvation” for “those who obey him” (v. 9)—successful obedience evidences effective ministry. Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `hebrews`.

### C13 — Beset with weakness includes sinfulness; Christ never “clothed/burdened” with such weakness
**Locus:** 2474–2476  
**Quote:** "Since, according to v. 3, the old high priest had to sacrifice for his own sins, this \"weakness\" included sinfulness. … Hebrews affirms the full humanity of Jesus, but it never says that he was \"clothed\" or \"burdened\" with \"weakness.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Heart of 2–3: sinful weakness causes inadequacy (2a) and self-sacrifice (3). Heart of 7–9 is v. 8: Christ “learned obedience through what he suffered”—life determined by godly obedience, not sinful weakness (cf. 4:15). Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `hebrews`.

### C14 — Aaron must offer for his own sins; new High Priest needs no self-offering for sin
**Locus:** 2478  
**Quote:** "Thus the Aaronic high priest's sacrifice for himself (v. 3) is clear evidence of his sinfulness (v. 2b) and therefore of his insufficiency (v. 2a). … There is no reason, then, to think that the all-sufficient new High Priest would have need to make such an offering for himself."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Third contrast on sacrifice: as/so construction stresses “for himself”; old order’s inadequacy confirmed later by 9:1–10. Christ’s effective self-offering for others is the contrast (v. 7). Target pages: `atonement`, `priesthood-of-christ`.

### C15 — Divine call required; Ps 2:7 + Ps 110:4 merge sonship and priesthood
**Locus:** 2480–2488  
**Quote:** "In Heb 5:5-6 the pastor offers Scriptural support for merging Christ's high priesthood with his sonship. The same God who declared him Son (Ps. 2:7), also declares him High Priest (Ps 110:4)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Fourth contrast: no self-appointment; “honor”/“glorify” language. Three oracles: Ps 2:7 sonship, Ps 110:1 exaltation, Ps 110:4 priesthood; 5:5–6 unites first and third. Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `melchizedek`, `hebrews`.

### C16 — Ps 110:4: legitimacy, exposure of Aaron, sufficiency because Son
**Locus:** 2492–2494  
**Quote:** "God's declaration that the One who is Son is a \"priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek\" (1) insures Christ's priestly legitimacy alongside that of Aaron (5:4-6); (2) exposes Aaron's priesthood as ineffective and antiquated (7:11-14); and (3) affirms the sufficiency of the ultimate High Priest because he is Son (7:15-25)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Association with Ps 2:7 / 110:1 suggests proclamation at exaltation; full exercise at session (8:1). Sacrifice analogies: Day of Atonement (High Priest before offering), consecration (fullness through offering/exaltation), covenant-establishing (benefits now available). Target pages: `melchizedek`, `priesthood-of-christ`, `atonement`.

### C17 — 5:7–10: consecration-sacrifice of total obedience unto death; Gethsemane-like but not restricted
**Locus:** 2496, 2516  
**Quote:** "This offering of total submission to God unto death is his sacrifice of priestly consecration. … Reference to Gethsemane is suggestive without being definitive. … It is better to see this entire verse as a depiction of the utter dependence upon God that characterized the Son's earthly life and came to its climax in Gethsemane and on the cross."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Verses 7–10 describe the Christ addressed as Son/Priest; sacrificial intent of “offered prayers and petitions” confirmed by high-priest offering framework (vv. 1, 3) and verb “offered.” Anticipates 10:5–10 (“I have come to do your will”). Object of prayer unspecified—intensifies total dependence; God able to save him “out of” death (resurrection). Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `atonement`, `hebrews`.

### C18 — “Heard because of godly fear,” not delivered merely from fear of death
**Locus:** 2522–2524

**Claim:** (Cockerill) Rejects reading that God only delivered Christ from fear of death (incongruous with “able to save him out of death”; different Greek from 2:15 “fear”). Session at right hand confirms acceptance (implies resurrection/exaltation). Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `atonement`.

### C19 — Although being Son, he learned obedience through suffering
**Locus:** 2526–2530

**Claim:** (Cockerill) V. 8 central to 7–9; active “learned obedience” vs passive “beset with weakness.” Sonship continued in incarnation (“Although being One who is Son”). Obedience grew richer unto the cross; antithesis of wilderness faithless disobedience. Death = climax of obedience and offering of obedient humanity. ### C20 — “Having been perfected” = vocational perfection; Source of eternal salvation for those who obey
**Locus:** 2534–2540  
**Quote:** "Salvation is not in a sacrifice but in a Savior. The eternal Son of God who was without defect has become \"perfected\" as the Savior of humankind. … this is a being perfected of vocation."

For “those who obey him,” not the “ignorant and going astray.” Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `atonement`, `hebrews`.

### C25 — Word of righteousness / mature: high-priestly appropriation trains discernment
**Locus:** 2582–2588  
**Quote:** "This \"word of righteousness\" is more than reasoning about what is right. It is the revelation of Christ's high priesthood as the means by which the pastor's hearers will be able to follow the \"righteous\" … and thus persevere in faithfulness."

Prefer “mature/maturity” over “perfect/perfection” in 5:14/6:1 because of infant contrast; yet root links to Christ’s being perfected and perfecting believers (cleansing + access). ### C26 — Leave elementary message; go on to maturity; “if God permits”
**Locus:** 2592–2600, 2618  
**Quote:** "This teaching is not false, but it is insufficient for perseverance in faith because it does not reveal the full sufficiency of Christ as the only Savior. … Though the pastor would urge his hearers to vigorous action, that action itself is possible only by yielding to the power of a gracious God."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “Word of the beginning of Christ” = basic Christian teachings (listed in 6:1–2), not Gospel biography; leave preoccupation, not discard truth. “Let us go on” may be passive “be carried on.” Advanced teaching (7–10) both for mature and produces maturity via cleansing, access, timely grace, New Covenant transformation. “If God permits” is real dependence and anticipates 6:4–8; do not presume on grace. Target pages: `hebrews`, `priesthood-of-christ`, `hebrews-warning-passages`.

### C27 — Six foundational items in three pairs; Jewish-continuity language
**Locus:** 2604–2614  
**Quote:** "Three pairs of genitive qualifiers describe this \"foundation\": (1) \"of repentance from dead works and faith in God\"; (2) \"of teaching about washings and the laying on of hands\"; (3) \"of resurrection of the dead and of eternal judgment.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) First pair = start of Christian life; third = outcome; second pair hard (plural “baptisms/washings” like 9:10; distinguish Christian baptism from Jewish washings; laying on of hands multi-use). Jewish terminology underlines one people of God through history; “dead works” = unbelief leading to loss (wilderness-like); “faith” always “faith in God.” No refuge in Old Covenant apart from Christ. Target pages: `hebrews`, `hebrews-warning-passages`.

### C28 — Warning 6:4–8: refusal to go on to maturity can end in irrevocable loss
**Locus:** 2624  
**Quote:** "Persistence in a state of spiritual regression, accompanied by the refusal to appropriate the pastor's teaching about Christ's high priesthood, leads to ultimate loss without possibility of restoration. … persistence in neglect of God's salvation springs from and reinforces unbelief. Thus it can lead to a definitive rejection of God's grace and the resultant irrevocable loss of his eternal blessings."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Warning is wake-up, not counsel of despair—hearers have not reached this end. Prepares for high-priestly teaching; 10:26–31 will be more forceful after full disclosure. Structure: vv. 4–6 people for whom repentance is impossible; vv. 7–8 land parable. Target pages: `hebrews-warning-passages`, `hebrews`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`.

### C29 — Five aorist participles under one article: unified description of the converted who later fall
**Locus:** 2628  
**Quote:** "One Greek article joins five aorist substantive participles in a unified description of those for whom repentance is impossible. … Because the first participle is emphasized by pride of place and by the qualifying \"once,\" … The next three participles are in apposition … The final participle, at the beginning of v. 6, stands in opposition to the others, \"and who have fallen away.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Five participles: (1) once enlightened; (2) tasted the heavenly gift; (3) become partakers of the Holy Spirit; (4) tasted the good word of God and the powers of the coming age; (5) fallen away. Postpone adynaton (“impossible”) until cause in v. 6. Target pages: `hebrews-warning-passages`, `hebrews`.

### C30 — Participles 1–4 = genuine conversion privileges, not mere instruction
**Locus:** 2630–2638  
**Quote:** "\"Those who have once been enlightened\" is a reference to conversion. … The next three participles can describe nothing less than the blessings experienced by the converted. … The metaphor \"taste\" is important because it demonstrates that those described have not just been taught about these realities but have truly experienced them."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “Once” stresses definitive enlightenment and anticipates irrepeatability of reconversion. Central: partakers of the Holy Spirit (cf. 2:4; salvation via Spirit-indwelling). Heavenly gift = great salvation in Christ; good word = quality of God’s faithful salvation-word; powers of coming age = miracles/Spirit as inaugural signs of salvation-age begun in high-priestly work, consummated at return. Taste = real present experience + foretaste of fulfillment; cumulative effect = comprehensive privilege and greater obligation. Explicitly: “have truly experienced a salvation.” Target pages: `hebrews-warning-passages`, `hebrews`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`.

### C31 — “Fallen away” = real apostasy of the genuinely converted (not conditional “might fall”)
**Locus:** 2642–2644  
**Quote:** "describing the same people who have been genuinely converted as having \"fallen away\" … If this participle were conditional, then the pastor would be describing the genuinely converted who might fall. The substantive is much more powerful: it describes the genuinely converted who have fallen. … The pastor is not referring to sin in general but to a repudiation of Christ and surrender of one's confession that sunders all connection with him."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Third-person description (not “you/we”) so hearers may still escape the fifth participle’s fate. Like wilderness turning “away from the living God” (3:12) and Esau “profane” (12:16). Aorist = complete apostasy culminating at a definite point. **Constructive stance (Arminian/Wesleyan trajectory, labels not used in body):** those once truly converted can definitively apostatize; readings that empty the participles of real conversion or make the fall only hypothetical of the unconverted are incompatible with this grammar and force of argument. Target pages: `hebrews-warning-passages`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`, `hebrews`.

### C32 — Re-crucifying and public shame: reason renewal is impossible
**Locus:** 2646–2648  
**Quote:** "Renewal is impossible because they are re-crucifying for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to public disgrace. … By \"crucifying\" Christ \"again\" these apostates have not subjected Christ to renewed suffering, but they have severed themselves from what Christ accomplished \"once for all\" (9:12; 10:10)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Prefers “crucify again/afresh” (Fathers/versions; context) over mere intensive “crucify up.” Apostasy severs from once-for-all work and publicly shames the Son; primary impossibility not mere psychological hardening but magnitude/finality of rejected once-for-all salvation—“Where, now, can they go for deliverance?” Target pages: `hebrews-warning-passages`, `atonement`, `priesthood-of-christ`.

### C33 — Adynaton rooted in God’s character (parallel to “impossible for God to lie,” 6:18)
**Locus:** 2650  
**Quote:** "Koester is right to locate the ultimate source of this impossibility in the character of God. … This divine impossibility is not a limitation on God's power but, like v. 18 below, a description of his character. … \"How, then, could we expect him to provide an alternate way of salvation for those who so definitively and publicly spurn his most gracious provision?\""

### C34 — Present participles: ongoing post-apostate stance; anxious hearers reassured
**Locus:** 2652  
**Quote:** "the postapostate life is also a continual \"re-crucifying of the Son of God and holding him up to public shame.\" This would imply that, in accord with the example of the wilderness generation, apostates do not seek repentance. … Those anxious for their own condition can be reassured, because the apostate would be unmoved by the pastor's warning."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Apostasy may be reached via drifting/neglect/obstinate resistance; thereafter unconcerned persistence in disobedience characterizes those beyond restoration. ### C35 — Land parable: same land, two harvests; apostasy of the apparently faithful is possible
**Locus:** 2656–2662  
**Quote:** "Both verses are about the same piece of land. Thus the pastor is not contrasting two parcels of \"land,\" but two \"harvests\" from the same land. … \"if it brings forth thorns and thistles.\" The apostasy of those who give every evidence of being faithful is possible. … \"Its destiny is burning.\" \"Burning\" betokens nothing short of eternal judgment."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Rain-fed land → useful fruit → blessing from God (covenant eternal gain, beyond mere agricultural logic); same land if thorns/thistles → worthless, near/subject to curse, destiny burning (eternal judgment). Blessing/curse language = eternal gain or loss. **Against “two classes of people never-overlapping” readings:** same-land conditional harvest underwrites real possibility that those who have drunk grace produce apostate fruit. Target pages: `hebrews-warning-passages`, `hebrews`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`.

### C36 — Scriptural echoes fill land picture with covenant gravity
**Locus:** 2664–2666  
**Quote:** "The ideas of this passage are closest to those of the Song of the Vineyard in Isa 5:1-7. … Many have noted the echoes of Deut 11:26-28 in Heb 6:7-8. … \"thorns and thistles\" … reminiscent of … Gen 3:17-18."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) No single OT source-context rigidly controlled; Isaiah vineyard (grace → expected fruit → judgment; in Hebrews inappropriate harvest only potential); Deut blessing/curse for hearing/refusing (links to 5:11 dull of hearing); Gen curse thorns; less likely Sodom fire. Covenant obedience/disobedience/blessing/cursing language reinforces eternal stakes of squandered grace. Target pages: `hebrews-warning-passages`, `hebrews`.

### C37 — Pastoral reassurance 6:9–12: “beloved,” better things pertaining to salvation
**Locus:** 2672–2680

### C38 — Twin foundations of confidence: God not unjust to forget; continuing love-work
**Locus:** 2682–2686  
**Quote:** "The pastor's confidence is founded on two of his favorite themes: the faithfulness of God and the corresponding faithfulness due from God's people. … \"For God is not unjust to forget your work.\" … their past demonstration of love continues into the present."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Work + love for God’s name shown in past and ongoing ministry to the saints (including costly support under persecution, 10:33–34). Love evidences sincere faith; still lack firm grasp of future promises and provision for attainment—pastor will supply. Past positive conduct motivates but does **not guarantee** future perseverance; assurance (9–10) preludes urgent exhortation (11–12). Target pages: `hebrews-warning-passages`, `hebrews`.

### C39 — Yearn for full assurance of hope until the end; do not become dull; imitate the faithful
**Locus:** 2688–2694  
**Quote:** "we yearn for each of you to demonstrate the same zeal for the full assurance of faith until the end, … in order that you might not become dull, but might become imitators of those who through faith and patience are inheriting the promises."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Pastoral longing for each individual; same zeal as love-service now directed to “full assurance of hope” maintained “until the end” (entry to Unshakable Kingdom at return). Climax of unit at 6:12: reverse 5:11 dullness by imitation of faith-and-patience heirs (plural → all of ch. 11; pair anticipates Abraham). “Inheriting the promises” = covenant/Promised-Land language fulfilled in eternal heavenly homeland through the Son. Target pages: `hebrews`, `hebrews-warning-passages`, `abraham`.

### C40 — Abraham oath unit: certify promises undergirding faith-and-patience
**Locus:** 2700–2702  
**Quote:** "The validity of this promise is ascertained by the testimony of Abraham (v. 15), by the oath of God (vv. 16-17), by the indisputable truthfulness of God's character (v. 18), and by its fulfillment in the privilege given the faithful of entering God's presence through their \"forerunner,\" who has become \"High Priest forever\" (vv. 19-20)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Abraham promise embodies all divine promises; oath to Abraham foreshadows oath-established priesthood (7:20–22). Abraham’s received blessings anticipate hearers’ reception through Christ’s priesthood. Target pages: `abraham`, `priesthood-of-christ`, `melchizedek`, `hebrews`.

### C41 — Gen 22:16–17 oath by himself; Abraham obtained by patience (earthly fulfillment)
**Locus:** 2704–2708  
**Quote:** "Verse 14 quotes this oath from Gen 22:17 … God swore by himself \"because he had no one greater by whom to swear.\" … The pastor is referring to Abraham's receiving more than a reconfirmation of the promise, but less than the heavenly homeland."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) After Akedah, God confirms promise with oath; Abraham’s testimony needs real earthly receipt (promised son Gen 21; Isaac received again Gen 22)—not mere reconfirmation, not yet 11:39–40 heavenly homeland (article of faith). “By having been patient” makes Abraham example for 6:12 and anticipates 11:1–40. Target pages: `abraham`, `hebrews`.

### C42 — Human oath conventions; God condescends to swear; two unchangeable things
**Locus:** 2710–2718  
**Quote:** "God's oath and his promise were the \"two unchangeable things\" by which he substantiated the \"unchangeable character\" of his gracious plan of salvation. … \"it was impossible for one who is God to lie.\" As in v. 4 above, this \"impossible\" is an affirmation of God's character, not a limitation on his power."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Humans swear by greater; oath ends controversy—God speaks human language of assurance. Causal “because God was desirous” = intense yearning to convince; “mediated/guaranteed by oath” anticipates Son as Guarantor (7:20–22). Twin impossibilities frame warning (v. 4) and assurance (v. 18). Purpose: strong encouragement for perseverance of “heirs of the promise.” Target pages: `abraham`, `hebrews`, `hebrews-warning-passages`, `priesthood-of-christ`.

**Locus:** 2722–2726

It also, however, moves forward \"entering into the inside of the\""

### C45 — Forerunner Jesus; High Priest forever after Melchizedek (return to deferred theme)
**Locus:** 2728–2734  
**Quote:** "where a forerunner on our behalf has entered in, even Jesus. … the phrase \"on our behalf\" indicates that the pastor has deliberately chosen the term \"forerunner\" to affirm that his entrance opens the way for the faithful to follow. … \"having become High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “Forerunner” (race/pilgrimage imagery; echoes pioneer 2:10) superior to Aaron—none followed Aaron inside; Jesus’ aorist entry opens way. Resumes postponed Melchizedekian theme from 5:10; substitutes “High Priest” for psalm’s “priest”; relocates “forever” to sentence end—eternity of Son as premise for incarnation/obedience/sacrifice/exaltation exposition in 7–10. Target pages: `priesthood-of-christ`, `melchizedek`, `hebrews`, `atonement`.

### C46 — Synthetic position on 6:4–8 (Cockerill’s constructive reading vs common alternatives)
**Locus:** 2624, 2630–2638, 2642–2644, 2650–2652, 2658  
**Quote:** "those who give every evidence of being faithful is possible" / "genuinely converted who have fallen" / "irrevocable loss of his eternal blessings" / "Those anxious for their own condition can be reassured"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill, composite from this range) (1) The five participles describe real conversion privileges (enlightenment, gift, Spirit, word, powers)—not mere outward profession empty of salvation. (2) “Fallen away” names actual apostates among the converted, not a merely conditional or hypothetical class of never-regenerate hearers. (3) Impossibility of re-repentance is real, grounded in God’s character and the finality of rejected once-for-all salvation (re-crucifying/public shame), ending in eternal curse/burning. (4) The same rain-soaked land can yield fruit or thorns—apostasy after experienced grace is possible. (5) The warning is pastoral and effective for the still-responsive; anxiety at it reassures; past faithfulness and God’s memory support confidence without making perseverance automatic. Body text does not name “Wesleyan-Arminian” or “Reformed” schools; the constructive options he affirms are the classic free-grace-with-real-apostasy reading, and the construals he excludes by grammar and parable (empty conversion; impossibility only psychological; two fixed lands/classes) are those typically used to protect unconditional final perseverance of every once-converted person. Target pages: `gareth-lee-cockerill`, `hebrews-warning-passages`, `hebrews`.
